source_read: PMC HTML (PMC7646282; Lancet Psychiatry 2019;6(5):427-436), opened in my own browser tab on 2026-10-27 (title checked); full page text saved to my folder and read start to end: Summary, Introduction with the Research in context panel, Methods (study design, participants, measures, statistical analysis, role of funder), Results with Tables 1-3, Discussion, acknowledgments, contributors, declaration of interests, reference list. No author-manuscript banner: the published version. Figures 1-3 are images: they could not be viewed during step 1 (the browser became unreachable after the text was saved); they were viewed on 2026-10-31 in a new tab of my own, after the card check, so the figure readings below are not blind (marked added_after_card_check). The supplementary appendix (mmc1.pdf) was not opened, as the brief requires. Step 1 and the card check were finished 2026-10-30 from the saved copy.

claims.overstatement: None with respect to this source. The claim attributes no figure to it; the design (first-episode case-control study plus a cross-site ecological correlation) cannot show causation, and the source's own attributable fractions are computed on the assumption of causality, which fits 'evidence is insufficient'.
claims.note: Qualifying role only. Editors' calculation from Table 2 (excess odds removed = (crude OR - adjusted OR) / (crude OR - 1)): daily use 58%, high potency 73%, ever use 79%, first use at 15 or younger 79%, low potency 90%, current use 94%. The 'crude' ORs are already weighted and adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity, so this measures only the further adjustment for education, employment, tobacco and other drugs; it is not comparable with the 45% (Moore et al., 2007), which starts from unadjusted estimates. The authors read their results causally (Research in context panel; Discussion, 12th paragraph) while stating that the attributable fractions assume causality (Methods, Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph). The selection-bias analysis (Results, 14th paragraph) addresses selection only, and its 'original' daily-use OR of 5.7 (4.4-7.5) matches no OR in Table 2.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (crude and fully adjusted OR columns) and its footnote
anchors.extracted: Crude ORs (weighted; adjusted only for age, gender, ethnicity) against fully adjusted ORs (adding education, employment, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs, hallucinogens): ever use 2.45 (2.0-2.9) to 1.3 (1.1-1.6); current use 2.7 (2.1-3.5) to 1.1 (0.9-1.5); first use at 15 or younger 3.9 (3.0-4.9) to 1.6 (1.1-2.1); daily use against never or occasional use 6.2 (4.8-8.2) to 3.2 (2.2-4.1); high potency 3.2 (2.6-4.0) to 1.6 (1.2-2.2); low potency 2.0 (1.6-2.5) to 1.1 (0.9-1.5). Editors' calculation: the added adjustment removed 58% (daily) to 94% (current use) of the excess odds.

anchors.locator: Methods > Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph; Summary > Methods; Research in context panel > Added value of this study; Discussion, 7th and 12th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Attributable fractions (Stata punafcc) are stated to assume causality. The authors nevertheless present the cross-site correlation as the first direct evidence that cannabis use affects variation in incidence and conclude that the findings confirm a harmful effect of daily and high-potency use; neither the case-control comparison nor the 10-site ecological correlation tests causation.

anchors.locator: Results, 14th paragraph (probabilistic sensitivity analysis)
anchors.extracted: Correction for selection bias (episensi; bias parameters in the appendix) gave a daily-use OR of 5.7 (3.5-9.4) against an original 5.7 (4.4-7.5); this concerns selection, not confounding, and the original OR matches neither the crude 6.2 (4.8-8.2) nor the adjusted 3.2 (2.2-4.1) in Table 2.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of direction or size, but two qualifiers are missing. (1) Exposure: 'daily use' here is the frequency of the person's most consistent lifetime pattern of use (Methods > Measures, 2nd paragraph), not current use; current use was not associated after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9-1.5, p = 0.36; Table 2). Suggest 'daily use as the most consistent pattern over the lifetime'. (2) Comparator: the 1.6 (1.1-2.1) for first use at 15 or younger is against people who never used (Table 2 footnote), which the claim does not say; against that reference it is close to the ever-use estimate of 1.3. 'Develop' is acceptable for incident first-episode cases, though the estimates are odds of case status in a case-control design.
claims.note: Checked against Table 2 and the Results text, all matching: 901 cases and 1,237 controls at 11 sites (London, Cambridge, Amsterdam, Gouda and Voorhout, Paris Val-de-Marne, Puy de Dome, Madrid, Barcelona, Bologna, Palermo, Ribeirao Preto); daily use 3.2 (2.2-4.1) against never or occasional use; more than once a week 1.4 (1.0-2.0), p = 0.066; ever use 1.3 (1.1-1.6); first use at 15 or younger 1.6 (1.1-2.1); daily use 3.1 (2.1-5.2) after adding age at first use; adjustment set as stated (Table 2 footnote). Daily use was reported by 29.5% of cases and 6.8% of controls, supporting 'reported more often'. The comparator for daily use is printed two ways: Table 2's reference row is never or occasional use, while the Summary, Results 7th paragraph and Discussion 1st paragraph say never users; the claim follows the table, the more cautious reading. Alcohol: Methods > Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph lists drinks per day among the confounders, but alcohol did not differ between groups (Results, 5th paragraph, p = 0.45) and is absent from the adjustment footnotes of Table 2 and Figure 1, so the 2019 models appear not to include it, which fits the claim's 'adjusted also for alcohol' for the 2015 study. The occasional-use ORs 0.84 (low potency) and 0.96 (high potency) are not in the text; Figure 1 (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check) shows them as 'rare use', with error bars spanning 1: confirmed. Controls were quota-sampled from address and GP lists and topped up through advertisements and leaflets for hard-to-reach groups, then weighted to census age, gender and ethnicity (Methods > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph): 'population controls' is the source's own term but includes some advertisement recruitment.

anchors.locator: Table 2, rows Lifetime frequency of use (Never or occasional use; Used more than once a week; Daily use), and footnote
anchors.extracted: Reference never or occasional use: 1061 controls (85.8%), 528 cases (58.7%). More than once a week: 92 (7.4%) vs 107 (11.9%), crude OR 2.5 (1.9-3.5), fully adjusted 1.4 (1.0-2.0), p = 0.066. Daily: 84 (6.8%) vs 266 (29.5%), crude 6.2 (4.8-8.2), fully adjusted 3.2 (2.2-4.1), p < 0.0001. Full adjustment: age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs, hallucinogens.

anchors.locator: Summary > Findings; Results, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The same daily-use estimate (adjusted OR 3.2, 2.2-4.1) is described against people who never used, whereas Table 2 prints never or occasional use as its reference; the Discussion gives 3.2 for daily use and 1.6 for high-potency use against never use.

anchors.locator: Table 2, row Lifetime cannabis use; Results, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ever use: 574 controls (46.4%) vs 585 cases (64.9%); crude OR 2.45 (2.0-2.9), fully adjusted 1.3 (1.1-1.6), p = 0.0225; described as a modest increase in odds; 13 missing in each group.

anchors.locator: Table 2, row First used cannabis age 15 or younger; Results, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: First use at 15 or younger: 169 controls (13.7%) vs 257 cases (28.6%); crude 3.9 (3.0-4.9), fully adjusted 1.6 (1.1-2.1), p = 0.0122, reference never users. The daily-use OR stayed near 3 after adding age at first use (3.1, 2.1-5.2), money spent (2.9, 1.9-4.4) or type used (2.6, 2.0-3.9). The authors state that early first use raised the odds modestly but not independently of frequency or potency.

anchors.locator: Methods > Measures, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, row Currently using cannabis
anchors.extracted: Lifetime frequency is defined as the frequency of the person's most consistent pattern of use. Current use: 132 controls (10.7%) vs 198 cases (22.0%); crude 2.7 (2.1-3.5), fully adjusted 1.1 (0.9-1.5), p = 0.36.

anchors.locator: Methods > Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Cases aged 18-64 at first presentation with ICD-10 F20-F33 psychosis, research diagnosis by OPCRIT, excluding organic (F09) and intoxication-related (F1X.5) psychosis; 1519 approached, 356 (23%) refused, 1130 took part. Controls by quota sampling (address and GP lists, plus advertisements and leaflets for hard-to-reach groups), 1499 recruited. Complete-case analysis after dropping Maison Blanche (no controls) and five sites with at least 10% missing data: 901 cases, 1237 controls, 11 sites.

anchors.locator: Figure 1 (fully adjusted bars, value labels)
anchors.extracted: Against never use, fully adjusted ORs: rare (occasional) use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (THC 10% or more), error bars spanning 1; use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57; daily use 2.19 and 4.78. Crude (age, gender, ethnicity) values 0.93, 1.11, 1.71, 2.12, 3.08 and 5.81. Intervals are not printed for the non-daily categories.

claims.overstatement: (1) The opening 'mainly using low-potency cannabis was not associated with psychosis' holds for low-potency use over all frequencies (1.1, 0.9-1.5), but in this source daily use of low-potency types was associated (2.2, 1.4-3.6), and the authors stress that the dose-response reflects daily use of traditional-strength types as well (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); the claim gives 2.19 later, but the opening sentence reads as if low-potency use carried no association at any frequency. (2) 'Most of all daily' fits the point estimates, but the source found no interaction between frequency and type (p = 0.25) and the two daily intervals overlap (2.5-6.3 and 1.4-3.6), so a larger risk for daily high-potency than daily low-potency use is not statistically shown. (3) 'Mainly' is not in the 2019 main text: Table 2 puts each person who ever used into one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, 3 missing; 251 + 334 = 585 cases), but how people who used both types were classed is described only in the appendix (not read). (4) Potency was assigned from Europe-wide (EMCDDA 2016) as well as national data on expected THC by type, not from national means alone.
claims.note: Checked and matching: 901 cases, 1,237 controls, 11 sites in the UK, Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil, May 2010 to April 2015; high-potency use in 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls (Table 2; Table 3 prints 35.1% and 19.1% for the same exposure in the whole sample); fully adjusted ORs against never use 1.6 (1.2-2.2) high, 1.1 (0.9-1.5) low; 1.5 (1.1-2.6) for high potency after controlling for daily use; daily high potency 4.8 (2.5-6.3) and daily low potency 2.2 (1.4-3.6) in the text (the claim's 4.78 and 2.19 round to these); site ORs for high potency 0.6 (Palermo) to 3.6 (Amsterdam), variation by site p = 0.45; attributable fraction 12.2% (3.0-16.1) assuming causality (Summary and Table 3; Results, 12th paragraph misprints the interval as 3.0-6.1). Editors' recomputation by Miettinen's formula (case prevalence x (OR - 1) / OR): 13.2% with Table 3's 35.1% (13.9% with Table 2's 37.1%) against the printed model-based 12.2%; daily use 20.3% against 20.4%; London high potency 30.0% against 30.3%; Amsterdam 50.3% as printed. 4.78, 2.19, the more-than-weekly 1.57 and 1.36 and the occasional 0.96 and 0.84 come only from Figure 1: confirmed there (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check). The 2019 paper calls the 2015 study its previous finding (reference 28) and cites its 24% figure, confirming the shared team; the London site's catchment is not named in the 2019 main text. Several printed 95% intervals are strongly asymmetric on the log scale (daily high potency 4.8, 2.5-6.3; whole-sample daily 3.2, 2.2-4.1; London daily 3.6, 1.4-4.4; Madrid daily 2.5, 2.1-7.3), which Wald intervals from a logistic model would not produce; the method for the intervals is not stated.

anchors.locator: Summary > Methods; Methods > Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Participants named the type of cannabis in their own words, with no question on potency; types were classed as low (THC below 10%) or high (10% or more) potency from expected THC in EMCDDA 2016 and national data. No biological verification of use; cannabidiol not included because reliable data existed only for England and the Netherlands; the authors note individual samples vary.

anchors.locator: Table 2, rows Lifetime use of cannabis by potency
anchors.extracted: Low potency: 331 controls (26.7%) vs 251 cases (27.9%), crude 2.0 (1.6-2.5), fully adjusted 1.1 (0.9-1.5), p = 0.38. High potency: 240 (19.4%) vs 334 (37.1%), crude 3.2 (2.6-4.0), fully adjusted 1.6 (1.2-2.2), p = 0.0032. Reference never users; potency missing for 3 controls.

anchors.extracted: High-potency use OR 1.5 (1.1-2.6) after controlling for daily use; starting high-potency use by age 15 OR 2.3 (1.4-3.1), no interaction (p = 0.63).

anchors.locator: Results, 9th paragraph; Summary > Findings
anchors.extracted: Combined frequency and type: daily high-potency use 4.8 (2.5-6.3) and daily low-potency use 2.2 (1.4-3.6) against never use; no interaction between frequency and type (p = 0.25).

anchors.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Table 3 (High-potency cannabis, by site)
anchors.extracted: ORs did not vary significantly by site for daily use (p = 0.25) or high-potency use (p = 0.45); high-potency ORs from 3.6 (1.5-7.7) in Amsterdam to 0.6 (0.1-2.5) in Palermo.

anchors.extracted: The authors replicate their previous south London finding (reference 28, the 2015 study) and cite its 24% attributable fraction for high-potency use; they add that the dose-response reflects not only high-potency use but also daily use of types with traditional THC levels.

anchors.extracted: Against never use, fully adjusted ORs: rare (occasional) use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (THC 10% or more), error bars spanning 1; use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57; daily use 2.19 and 4.78. Crude (age, gender, ethnicity) values 0.93, 1.11, 1.71, 2.12, 3.08 and 5.81. Intervals are not printed for the non-daily categories.

claims.overstatement: The claim's 'ecological correlation' is the right description; the source's own wording overstates (it presents the cross-site correlation as the first direct evidence that cannabis use affects variation in incidence). Not supported as worded: 'two strongly overlapping measures' (see note).
claims.note: Supported: incidence adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity correlated with the prevalence of daily use among controls (r = 0.8, p = 0.0109) and of high-potency use (r = 0.7, p = 0.0286); 10 sites, because Figure 3 omits Puy-de-Dome (no adjusted rate), although the Summary and Results 16th paragraph say 11. The printed p-values fit 10 sites: with 8 degrees of freedom they correspond to r of about 0.76 and 0.69, whereas r = 0.8 at 11 sites would give p of about 0.003. Not supported as worded: the source states that the two prevalences were only modestly correlated (r = 0.2, p = 0.0413; Results, 16th paragraph). That printed pair cannot hold at 10-11 sites (r = 0.2 gives p of about 0.56-0.58; p = 0.041 needs about 100 observations). The editors' recomputation from the site prevalences in Table 3 gives r = 0.71 (10 sites, p about 0.02) or 0.73 (11 sites, p about 0.011), which agrees with the claim's description. The claim should label the overlap an editors' calculation from Table 3 and mention the printed r = 0.2, or drop it. Minor: Bologna's daily-use prevalence is 3 of 65 controls (4.6%) in the text but 4.1% in Table 3. Figure 3 (viewed 2026-10-31, after the card check) gives the same picture: from the plotted points, daily use and high-potency use among controls correlate at r of about 0.71-0.76.

anchors.locator: Summary > Findings; Methods > Statistical analysis, 6th paragraph; Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs; Figure 3 caption
anchors.extracted: Pearson correlation across sites of incidence adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity with prevalence among controls: daily use r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109), high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286). Puy-de-Dome has no adjusted rate (ethnicity missing for 27 of 42 incident cases), so 10 sites are plotted. Examples: London daily use 26 of 223 controls (11.7%), incidence 45.7 per 100,000 person-years; Amsterdam 13 of 100 (13.0%), 37.9; Bologna 3 of 65 (4.6%), 21.0; Paris high-potency use 21 of 100, 46.1.

anchors.locator: Results, 16th paragraph (last sentence)
anchors.extracted: The authors report that the prevalences of daily use and of high-potency use among controls were only modestly correlated, r = 0.2, p = 0.0413, and therefore show both.

anchors.locator: Table 3, column Prevalence of exposure in controls (High-potency and Daily rows by site)
anchors.extracted: Editors' calculation: across the sites, control prevalence of high-potency use (1.5% to 54.0%) and of daily use (4.0% to 13.1%) correlate at r = 0.71 (10 sites without Puy de Dome) or 0.73 (all 11).

anchors.locator: Research in context panel > Evidence before this study
anchors.extracted: The panel describes a south London study (Boydell and colleagues) as speculating that a rise in schizophrenia incidence between 1965 and 1999 might relate to the rise in cannabis use in the year before first presentation; no magnitude given (second-hand).

anchors.locator: Research in context panel > Added value of this study; Discussion, 7th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors call the cross-site correlation the first evidence that differences in daily and high-potency use contribute to variation in incidence, and the first direct evidence of an effect on incidence; the design is ecological.

anchors.locator: Figure 3, panels A and B (site points, read on screen; approximate)
anchors.extracted: 10 sites plotted (London, Cambridge, Amsterdam, Gouda and Voorhout, Madrid, Barcelona, Paris, Bologna, Palermo, Ribeirao Preto). Editors' calculation from the plotted points: daily-use prevalence vs adjusted incidence r of about 0.76-0.78, high-potency prevalence vs incidence about 0.72, and daily vs high-potency prevalence about 0.71-0.76, so the two exposures overlap strongly, against the r = 0.2 printed in the text.

key_findings.note: The Maison Blanche exclusion is stated in Results, 2nd paragraph; the five sites with missing data and the 901/1237 totals in the 3rd. Editors' arithmetic confirmed: 229 of 1130 cases (20.3%) and 262 of 1499 controls (17.5%) not analysed.
Reference-group arithmetic confirmed: 1061 - 650 = 411 controls and 528 - 303 = 225 cases in the never-or-occasional reference had used cannabis (approximate, as 13 per group lack ever-use data).

All numbers match Table 2 and Results, 8th paragraph. The word 'mainly' does not appear in the main text, where the measure is lifetime use of cannabis by potency; each person who ever used is in one class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, 3 missing; 251 + 334 = 585 cases), but how people who used both types were classed is described only in the appendix (not read). Keep 'mainly' only if the appendix confirms it.

Checked on 2026-10-31 at Figure 1 (after the card check, at the stated place): adjusted 0.84, 0.96, 1.36, 1.57, 2.19, 4.78 and crude 0.93, 1.11, 1.71, 2.12, 3.08, 5.81, with the 'rare use' labels, as stated; text gives 4.8 (2.5-6.3), 2.2 (1.4-3.6) and p = 0.25.
Checked on 2026-10-31 at Figure 2: daily high-potency 5.16 (London), 9.43 (Amsterdam), 4.28 (Paris), legend counts as stated; the error bars read roughly as the card says.
Editors' check confirmed for every site: printed fractions are within 1.0 percentage point of the case-based formula (largest gap, whole-sample high potency: 13.2% calculated vs 12.2% printed).

Recomputed: the printed p-values fit r of about 0.76 and 0.69 with 10 sites; with 11 sites, p = 0.0109 corresponds to r of about 0.73. Figure 3 viewed 2026-10-31: 10 sites plotted, Puy de Dome absent.

reporting_issues.note: Also the Results, 7th paragraph describes the daily-use comparison against never use.
Recomputed (8 degrees of freedom): p = 0.0109 corresponds to r of about 0.76, and p = 0.0286 to about 0.69.

Recomputed from Table 3's control prevalences: r = 0.71 for the 10 plotted sites (p of about 0.02) and 0.73 for all 11 (p of about 0.011); r = 0.2 gives p of about 0.58 (10 sites) or 0.56 (11). The plotted points of Figure 3 give r of about 0.76 for the same pair.
The Bologna and London counts are in Results, 15th paragraph, and the 230 and 101 in the Figure 2 legend, as stated.

Checked on 2026-10-31 at Figure 3 (reading the points on screen): Paris incidence plotted at about 41.7, below London at about 45.8 (text 46.1 vs 45.7); daily-use prevalence plotted at about 6% for Barcelona and 10% for Paris (Table 3: 8.3% and 11.6%); also Madrid about 11% (Table 3: 10.5%).
Recomputed: t of about 22.8 if 0.4 is an SD; t of about 0.71 (p of about 0.48) if it is a standard error.
Recomputed geometric centres: 3.0, 3.97, 2.48 and 3.92. Others are lopsided too, e.g. Gouda and Voorhout daily use 2.8 (1.4-20.3) and Paris high potency 2.1 (0.8-3.6).

The problem is general, not limited to the three sites marked significant: every site-level fraction in Table 3 has an interval above zero, including 15 whose odds-ratio interval includes 1 (for example Madrid high potency 2.0, 0.7-5.7, with 17.2%, 0.9-25.0; Puy de Dome daily use 1.1, 0.4-12.2, with 1.2%, 0.8-15.4).
Reference 3 is a review of marijuana legalization and its impact on physicians and public health (Wilkinson et al., 2016), as stated.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high follows from the confounding domain: adjustment for measured confounders roughly halves every odds ratio, and family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning and use during a prodrome were not addressed. Exposure measurement at some concerns is defensible, though retrospective recall after onset, with potency inferred from the name of the type, could justify high; it does not change the overall judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits, and points (1) to (7) are accurate against the text (Discussion, 3rd paragraph calls high-potency use a strong predictor in Paris; Discussion, 11th paragraph says unmentioned recruitment materials avoid selection and recall bias). One addition: the Results also use causal and risk wording for odds ratios (high-potency use increased the odds, 8th paragraph; a doubling of risk, 8th paragraph; a fourfold increase in risk, 9th paragraph).

missed: Every site-level attributable-fraction interval in Table 3 lies above zero, including 15 site estimates whose odds-ratio interval includes 1, so reporting issue 10 applies to the whole table, not only to the three entries marked significant.

'Mainly' high- or low-potency use (key finding 6, can_establish, analysis, interpretation_gap) is not in the main text, which speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency; the rule for classing people who used both types is only in the appendix. Drop 'mainly' or cite the appendix after reading it.

The Discussion (1st paragraph) says early first use did not raise the odds independently of frequency or potency, but no estimate for first use at 15 or younger adjusted for daily use or potency is printed; only the reverse adjustment (daily use 3.1, 2.1-5.2, after adding age at first use) and the high-potency-by-15 estimate (2.3, 1.4-3.1) are given.

Current use at assessment was not associated after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9-1.5, p = 0.36; in key finding 3), which matters for claims that speak of people who use cannabis without saying that the exposure is a lifetime pattern; worth stating in the exposure field beside the definition of lifetime frequency.
